title: 12. Cloud, Containers & Deployment: PaaS (Platform as a Service)
summary: PaaS is a cloud service model where the provider delivers a managed platform — operating system, runtime, middleware, and deployment pipeline — so the customer can ship application code without provisioning or patching the…
objectives: What distinguishes PaaS from IaaS at the contract level, and why does the distinction matter operationally?
Explain how a buildpack works and why it is central to the PaaS deployment experience.
What is the Procfile, and what problem does it solve?
How does PaaS handle scaling, and what are the limits compared to IaaS?

sections.title: Explanation
sections.body:
> **In one line:** PaaS is a cloud service model where the provider delivers a managed platform — operating system, runtime, middleware, and deployment pipeline — so the customer can ship application code without provisioning or patching the underlying infrastructure.
Platform as a Service occupies the middle ground of the cloud service spectrum, and it exists because most application teams do not actually want to manage operating systems. They want to write code, push it, and have it run. Heroku, launched in 2007, was the first PaaS to make this concrete: you typed `git push heroku main`, Heroku detected the language, built a slug, attached it to a Dyno, and your app was live on the internet within minutes. App Engine, Elastic Beanstalk, Azure App Service, Render, Fly.io, and Vercel all followed the same fundamental contract — the platform owns the OS and runtime, the customer owns the application code, and the deployment pipeline is the platform's product. Snapchat's early years ran on Google App Engine precisely because a tiny team could not operate servers; they pushed Python code and App Engine scaled it to millions of users without them ever touching a kernel patch.

The defining property of PaaS is the deployment abstraction. Where IaaS exposes VMs, security groups, and volumes, PaaS exposes applications, environments, and add-ons. You do not launch instances; you `git push` or `cf push`, and the platform decides how many containers to run, where to place them, and how to load-balance them. Heroku's `Procfile` — a single text file declaring process types like `web: gunicorn app:app` and `worker: celery -A app worker` — is the canonical expression of this abstraction. The platform reads the Procfile, provisions the right number of Dynos per process type, binds them to a router, and exposes a single HTTPS endpoint. The trade-off is that you cannot tune the kernel, cannot install custom system packages, and cannot choose an unsupported runtime version. Most application teams consider this an excellent trade.

The second property is auto-scaling by default. On IaaS, you build an auto-scaling group, write scaling policies, and tune them over weeks. On PaaS, scaling is a config knob: `heroku ps:scale web=10` scales the web process to ten instances, and most platforms support autoscaling rules based on request latency or queue depth. App Engine's automatic scaling reads traffic and adds or removes instances to keep latency under a target threshold — the developer specifies desired latency, the platform handles the rest. This is dramatically simpler than self-managed autoscaling and is one of the main reasons small teams pick PaaS. The trade-off is that scaling is coarser (you scale process types, not individual instances) and the platform's autoscaling algorithms may not fit unusual traffic patterns.

The third property is managed add-ons. Every PaaS has a marketplace of backing services — Postgres, Redis, Elasticsearch, S3-compatible object storage — exposed as environment variables. `heroku addons:create heroku-postgresql:hobby-dev` provisions a managed Postgres and exposes `DATABASE_URL` to your app instantly. This eliminates the operational burden of running a database: backups, failover, version upgrades, and replication are all the provider's problem. The trade-off is cost: a Heroku Postgres Standard-0 ($50/month) is roughly 5x the price of an equivalent RDS instance, and at scale most teams eventually migrate to IaaS-managed databases to cut cost. But for an early-stage product, the speed of having a managed database in 30 seconds is worth the markup.

The fourth property is buildpacks and container detection. Modern PaaS platforms detect the application's language via files in the repository (`requirements.txt` for Python, `package.json` for Node, `go.mod` for Go) and use a buildpack to compile it into a runnable artifact. Heroku's buildpacks were the inspiration for Cloud Native Buildpacks, now an OCI standard. Elastic Beanstalk and App Engine follow the same pattern. More recent platforms — Render, Fly.io, Vercel — accept a `Dockerfile` directly, blurring the line between PaaS and container orchestration but preserving the deployment abstraction: you push, the platform builds and runs. This convergence is deliberate: the customer cares about "my code is live," not about the container runtime.

The fifth property, and the one that determines whether PaaS is the right choice, is the abstraction ceiling. PaaS is wonderful when your workload fits the platform's model: stateless web apps, background workers, scheduled jobs. It becomes painful when you need something the platform does not support: a custom kernel module, a GPU for ML inference, a long-lived WebSocket with sticky sessions, a stateful service that needs persistent local disk. Heroku's Cedar stack famously did not support WebSockets for years, forcing real-time apps onto alternative platforms. The discipline is to recognize when you have hit the ceiling and migrate just the affected service to IaaS, keeping the rest on PaaS. Most startups follow this trajectory: start 100% on Heroku or App Engine, migrate the heaviest services to EC2 or Kubernetes as they hit limits, and end up with a hybrid footprint.

The trade-off summary: PaaS trades control and per-unit cost for speed of delivery and reduced operational burden. For a five-person startup shipping an MVP, PaaS is almost always the right choice — the engineering time saved by not operating servers is worth more than the cloud bill markup. For a 500-person company running hundreds of services with heterogeneous requirements, PaaS becomes a limiting factor and IaaS or managed Kubernetes takes over. The interesting middle ground is "PaaS-like abstractions on top of Kubernetes" — Render, Fly.io, and Vercel are exactly this, providing PaaS ergonomics while running on top of Kubernetes or Firecracker microVMs. The long-run trajectory of the industry is toward PaaS-like experiences for application teams, with the heavy infra managed by a smaller and smaller group of specialists.

### Mermaid Diagram
```mermaid
flowchart LR
    Dev[Developer] -->|git push| PaaS[PaaS Control Plane]
    PaaS -->|detect language| BP[Buildpack / Dockerfile]
    BP -->|build slug/image| REG[Artifact Registry]
    REG -->|deploy| R1[Dyno/Container 1]
    REG -->|deploy| R2[Dyno/Container 2]
    REG -->|deploy| R3[Dyno/Container 3]
    Router[Platform Router] --> R1
    Router --> R2
    Router --> R3
    User[End User] -->|HTTPS| Router
    R1 -.->|env var| DB[(Managed Postgres add-on)]
    R2 -.->|env var| DB
    R3 -.->|env var| DB
    PaaS -->|autoscale| Router
```

### ASCII Diagram
```
+---------------------------------------------------+
|  PaaS Provider (Heroku / App Engine / Beanstalk)  |
|                                                   |
|  Developer  --git push-->  Build Pipeline         |
|                              |                    |
|                              v                    |
|                        +-----------+              |
|                        | Buildpack |  detects     |
|                        | / Docker  |  language    |
|                        +-----------+              |
|                              |                    |
|                              v                    |
|                        +-----------+              |
|                        |  Slug /   |  artifact    |
|                        |  Image    |              |
|                        +-----------+              |
|                              |                    |
|                +-------------+-------------+      |
|                v             v             v      |
|          +---------+   +---------+   +---------+  |
|          | Dyno 1  |   | Dyno 2  |   | Dyno 3  |  |
|          | web app |   | web app |   | worker  |  |
|          +---------+   +---------+   +---------+  |
|                ^             ^                    |
|                |             |                    |
|              Platform Router <-- HTTPS -- User    |
|                                                   |
|  Add-ons (env-var injected):                      |
|    DATABASE_URL -> managed Postgres               |
|    REDIS_URL    -> managed Redis                  |
|    S3_BUCKET    -> managed object store           |
+---------------------------------------------------+
```

### Walkthrough
1. The developer pushes code to the PaaS git endpoint (or connects a GitHub repo); the platform's control plane receives the push and starts a build.
2. A buildpack or Dockerfile compiles the code into a runnable artifact (slug or image), which is stored in a registry and versioned by commit SHA.
3. The platform's router rolls the new artifact out across N process containers (Dynos, instances), health-checks them, and switches traffic once they are ready — the developer never touches a load balancer.
4. Backing services (Postgres, Redis, object storage) are provisioned as add-ons and exposed as environment variables; the platform handles their backups, failover, and upgrades invisibly to the application.

sections.title: Code
sections.body:
**What this code covers**

- Detects the language and produces build commands.
- Mimics git push paas main: detect, build, release, scale.
- Mimics heroku ps:scale web=N.
- Toy autoscaler: if p95 latency > target, scale web by 1.
- Paas_deploy.py - runnable mock of a PaaS control plane.
- Models: push -> detect -> build -> release -> scale -> route.
- Release phase: stop old dynos, start new ones per Procfile
- Pretend we measured latency

**Defines:** `Build`, `Dyno`, `AddOn`, `Buildpack`, `PaaS`

```python
# paas_deploy.py - runnable mock of a PaaS control plane.
# Models: push -> detect -> build -> release -> scale -> route.
from dataclasses import dataclass, field
from typing import List, Dict, Optional
import uuid, time, hashlib, random

@dataclass
class Build:
    build_id: str
    commit_sha: str
    language: str
    artifact_url: str
    status: str = "queued"   # queued -> building -> succeeded -> failed

@dataclass
class Dyno:
    dyno_id: str
    process_type: str        # web, worker, clock...
    build_id: str
    state: str = "starting"  # starting -> up -> crashed -> stopped
    port: Optional[int] = None

@dataclass
class AddOn:
    name: str
    kind: str                # postgres, redis, s3
    env_vars: Dict[str, str] = field(default_factory=dict)

class Buildpack:
    """Detects the language and produces build commands."""
    DETECT = {
        "requirements.txt": "python",
        "package.json":     "nodejs",
        "go.mod":           "go",
        "Gemfile":          "ruby",
        "Dockerfile":       "docker",
    }
    @classmethod
    def detect(cls, repo_files: List[str]) -> str:
        for f, lang in cls.DETECT.items():
            if f in repo_files:
                return lang
        raise RuntimeError("no supported language detected")

class PaaS:
    def __init__(self, app_name: str):
        self.app_name = app_name
        self.builds: Dict[str, Build] = {}
        self.dynos: Dict[str, Dyno] = {}
        self.addons: Dict[str, AddOn] = {}
        self.release: Optional[str] = None   # current release build_id

    def push(self, commit_sha: str, repo_files: List[str],
             procfile: Dict[str, str]) -> Build:
        """Mimics `git push paas main`: detect, build, release, scale."""
        print(f"\n[push] {self.app_name} commit={commit_sha[:8]}")
        lang = Buildpack.detect(repo_files)
        bid = "b-" + uuid.uuid4().hex[:8]
        build = Build(bid, commit_sha, lang, f"registry/{self.app_name}:{commit_sha[:8]}")
        self.builds[bid] = build
        print(f"  detected language: {lang}")

        # build phase
        build.status = "building"
        time.sleep(0.05)
        build.status = "succeeded"
        print(f"  built artifact: {build.artifact_url}")

        # release phase: stop old dynos, start new ones per Procfile
        for d in self.dynos.values():
            d.state = "stopped"
        self.dynos.clear()
        for ptype, cmd in procfile.items():
            for _ in range(2 if ptype == "web" else 1):
                did = "d-" + uuid.uuid4().hex[:8]
                port = random.randint(5000, 5999) if ptype == "web" else None
                dyno = Dyno(did, ptype, bid, port=port)
                self.dynos[did] = dyno
                time.sleep(0.02)
                dyno.state = "up"
                print(f"  dyno up: {did} type={ptype} cmd='{cmd}' port={port}")

        self.release = bid
        print(f"  release {bid} now live, router bound")
        return build

    def scale(self, process_type: str, count: int):
        """Mimics `heroku ps:scale web=N`."""
        existing = [d for d in self.dynos.values()
                    if d.process_type == process_type and d.state == "up"]
        diff = count - len(existing)
        if diff > 0:
            for _ in range(diff):
                did = "d-" + uuid.uuid4().hex[:8]
                dyno = Dyno(did, process_type, self.release,
                            port=random.randint(5000, 5999) if process_type=="web" else None)
                self.dynos[did] = dyno
                dyno.state = "up"
        elif diff < 0:
            for d in existing[:abs(diff)]:
                d.state = "stopped"
        live = [d for d in self.dynos.values() if d.process_type == process_type and d.state=="up"]
        print(f"[scale] {process_type}={len(live)} (desired {count})")

    def add_addon(self, kind: str, plan: str = "hobby") -> AddOn:
        name = f"{kind}-{self.app_name}"
        url = f"{kind}://user:pass@{kind}-{uuid.uuid4().hex[:6]}.internal:5432/db"
        addon = AddOn(name=name, kind=kind,
                      env_vars={f"{kind.upper()}_URL": url, f"{kind.upper()}_PLAN": plan})
        self.addons[kind] = addon
        print(f"[addon] {kind} provisioned, env var injected")
        return addon

    def autoscale_by_latency(self, target_ms: int = 200):
        """Toy autoscaler: if p95 latency > target, scale web by 1."""
        # pretend we measured latency
        measured = random.randint(80, 400)
        if measured > target_ms:
            print(f"[autoscale] p95={measured}ms > {target_ms}ms, scaling web +1")
            self.scale("web", len([d for d in self.dynos.values()
                                   if d.process_type=="web" and d.state=="up"]) + 1)

if __name__ == "__main__":
    app = PaaS("snap-clone")
    app.add_addon("postgres")
    app.add_addon("redis")
    app.push(commit_sha=hashlib.sha1(b"v1").hexdigest(),
             repo_files=["requirements.txt", "app.py", "Procfile"],
             procfile={"web": "gunicorn app:app", "worker": "celery -A app worker"})
    app.scale("web", 4)
    app.autoscale_by_latency(target_ms=200)
    print(f"final: {len(app.dynos)} dynos, release={app.release[:10]}")
```

Heroku's router times out requests at 30 seconds on all Dyno tiers, and this is a hard limit that cannot be configured away.
The contract-level difference is what the provider manages. In IaaS, the provider manages up to the hypervisor; the customer manages the guest OS, runtime, and app.
quiz.explanation: The contract-level difference is what the provider manages. In IaaS, the provider manages up to the hypervisor; the customer manages the guest OS, runtime, and app. In PaaS, the provider manages up to the runtime; the customer manages only the application code.
